Factor Scores With Standard Errors, Intervals, and Determinacy

Source: R/factor_scores.R
factor_scores.Rd

Computes, for every row given to a fitted lavaan model and every latent variable, both standard factor scores: the regression score (Thomson, 1934; Thurstone, 1935) and the Bartlett score (Bartlett, 1937, 1938). Each comes with a per-case standard error and confidence interval, beside the number of the factor's items the case answered, the case's missing data pattern, and the determinacy of each score for that pattern (the correlation of the score with the factor it stands for). For ordered items the two scores are their categorical counterparts in lavaan, the empirical Bayes modal (EBM) score and the maximum likelihood (ML) score.

Usage

factor_scores(fit, data = NULL, conf_level = 0.95)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_factor_scores'
print(x, n = 3L, digits = getOption("dmar.digits", 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_factor_scores'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_factor_scores'
glance(x, ...)

Arguments

fit

A fitted lavaan model (from lavaan::cfa(), lavaan::sem(), or fa_confirmatory(output = "fit")) estimated from raw data. A fit to summary statistics (it holds no rows) and a fit that did not converge are refused, as are a two-level fit, a fit of continuous items that keeps incomplete cases without FIML (two-stage maximum likelihood, pairwise deletion or the available cases) and is conditional on exogenous covariates, a fit with regressions among the variables lavaan holds as latent in which the disturbance of an observed variable regressed on others covaries with a factor (an observed mediator, for one), a fit conditional on exogenous covariates with regressions and an observed variable that lavaan holds among the latent variables but regresses on nothing, and, with ordered items, a fit with a direct effect of an exogenous covariate on an observed variable that also depends on a factor directly, one with a regression on an observed variable that is not an exogenous covariate when the variable predicted also depends on a factor directly, the predictor is ordered, or, in a row the fit keeps, the predictor is missing where the variable predicted is observed and depends on a factor through no variable the row has observed, one with an observed variable whose disturbance covaries with a factor and whose row lavaan keeps among the loadings, one with exogenous covariates that is not conditional on them, and any fit under a lavaan older than 0.7-3 (see Details). A fit with ordered items and residual covariances is scored with a warning. For continuous unconditional fits, a disturbance related only to an observed conditioning variable leaves the factor's regression conditional mean valid. Its scores and intervals are retained; Bartlett scores, SEs, limits, and determinacy are NA with the reason when their stronger conditional-unbiasedness requirement fails.

data

Optional but recommended: the data frame given to the model, with the same rows in the same order (extra columns are ignored). It is checked against the data the model holds (every observed variable present, the same number of rows, and the same values in the rows the model used), and a frame that differs is refused. With it, the table has one row for every row of data, including rows the fit did not use (deleted listwise, or with a missing group), and their reason and items answered are filled in; for a multiple group fit it must hold the group variable. Without it, the table runs from row 1 to the last row the fit holds, so rows at the end of the data that the fit did not use are not represented, and the reason given a row the fit did not use cannot say which of its values was missing. The scores are always those of the rows the fit was estimated from; scoring new observations is not what this function does.

conf_level

Confidence level for the per-case intervals; defaults to 0.95.

x

A dmar_factor_scores table returned by factor_scores().

n

For print(), the number of rows shown for each factor (default 3); the pattern table shows up to 4 * n rows. knit_print.dmar_tbl and as_kable show the same summary with the default.

digits

For print(), the decimal places of the scores, their standard errors and limits, and the determinacies (default getOption("dmar.digits", 3); see dmar_tbl).

...

Unused.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_factor_scores, dmar_tbl) with one row for each row of the data and each factor, ordered by factor and then row, so that x$.derived_bartlett[x$factor == "f"] lines up with the rows of data. Its columns are always the same: row (the row of the data), group (the group label; NA for a fit without groups), factor, .derived_regression, .derived_regression_se, .derived_regression_ci_lower, .derived_regression_ci_upper, .derived_bartlett, .derived_bartlett_se, .derived_bartlett_ci_lower, .derived_bartlett_ci_upper, items_observed and items (the factor's items the case answered, and its number of items; a higher order factor's items are those of the factors it measures, and a loading the model holds at zero, written 0*x or a*x with a == 0 directly or through a chain of equalities, makes no item: the scores and reasons are those of the model without it), pattern (the missing data pattern of the variables scored from, within the group, numbered from the most complete), determinacy_regression, determinacy_bartlett (for the case's pattern), and reason (empty, or why a value is missing or borrowed; reasons are separated by semicolons). The .derived_regression and .derived_bartlett columns hold the EBM and ML scores for ordered items.

The eight columns that hold the scores, their standard errors, and their confidence limits carry the prefix .derived_, so that a score joined to the observed data cannot be taken for an observed variable or collide with one (a data set may well have a column named regression). The derived_columns attribute names them by what each holds (regression, regression_se, regression_ci_lower, regression_ci_upper, and the same four for bartlett), so x[[attr(x, "derived_columns")[["bartlett"]]]] is the column of Bartlett scores. All are present under every supported model.

Attributes: methods (the lavaan methods behind the two columns), conf_level, estimator, missing, patterns (one row per group, pattern, and factor: the number of cases, the items observed, the variables missing, both determinacies, min_score_correlation, and both standard errors), determinacy (per group and factor, for complete data: both determinacies and min_score_correlation), scored_from ("fit" or "indicators"), auxiliary (the auxiliary variables set aside), ngroups, and lavaan_version. tidy() returns the table as a plain data frame; glance() returns one row with the numbers of rows, rows scored, factors, groups, and patterns, the two methods, the estimator, the missing data treatment, scored_from, and conf_level.

Details

Both scores are returned because neither is better in general; which one belongs in a later analysis depends on the role the factor plays there (see Which Score Belongs Where). For relations among factors, the scores are rarely the right tool at all: a latent variable model, estimated in one step or by structural after measurement (lavaan::sam(); Rosseel & Loh, 2024), estimates them without the bias a regression among scores carries. The scores are for what only scores can do: describe and rank individual cases, carry a factor into an analysis outside the model, or check the model's assumptions case by case. Requires lavaan.

The Two Scores. For the observed items \(o\) of a case, with \(\Lambda_o\) their rows of the loading matrix, \(\Theta_{oo}\) their residual covariance matrix, \(\Phi\) the model implied covariance matrix of the factors, \(\Sigma_{oo} = \Lambda_o \Phi \Lambda_o' + \Theta_{oo}\), and \(\mu_o\) the model implied item means, $$\hat{\eta}_R = \mathrm{E}(\eta) + \Phi \Lambda_o' \Sigma_{oo}^{-1} (y_o - \mu_o)$$ is the regression score, the mean of the factor's distribution given the observed items under the normal factor model, and $$\hat{\eta}_B = \mathrm{E}(\eta) + (\Lambda_o' \Theta_{oo}^{-1} \Lambda_o)^{-1} \Lambda_o' \Theta_{oo}^{-1} (y_o - \mu_o)$$ is the Bartlett score, the generalized least squares (and, under normality, maximum likelihood) estimate of the case's factor value treated as a fixed quantity. The regression score is shrunk toward the factor mean, by more when the items carry less information, and so has the smaller mean squared error; the Bartlett score is not shrunk, so its expected value given the case's factor value is that value (conditionally unbiased; under missing data this needs a condition on why values are missing, see Missing Data), at the price of a larger variance. Their standard errors differ in kind: that of the regression score is the posterior standard deviation, the square root of the diagonal of \(\Phi - \Phi \Lambda_o' \Sigma_{oo}^{-1} \Lambda_o \Phi\), and that of the Bartlett score is its sampling standard error given the case's factor value, the square root of the diagonal of \((\Lambda_o' \Theta_{oo}^{-1} \Lambda_o)^{-1}\). The scores and their standard errors are those of lavaan::lavPredict() with se = "standard", aligned to the rows of the data (with auxiliary variables, the same formulas applied to the indicators alone; see below).

The Bartlett score of a factor exists only when the observed items identify the factor's value, that is, when the factor's unit vector lies in the row space of \(\Lambda_o\), so that its value is a function of the items' expected values. With simple structure that holds for every factor with an observed item. With items shared among factors (cross-loadings, a bifactor model) a pattern can fail it: a case that answered one item loading on two factors, and nothing else of either, has items that do not separate the two. The matrix \(\Lambda_o' \Theta_{oo}^{-1} \Lambda_o\) is then singular, and lavaan falls back on a generalized inverse, whose minimum norm solution is not an estimate of either factor's value and whose standard error is not the error of anything; such a factor's Bartlett score, standard error, and determinacy are NA here with the reason. A factor the pattern does identify keeps its score, which the generalized inverse gives uniquely.

Which Score Belongs Where. Using scores in place of factors in a later regression (factor score regression) with the same type of score on both sides gives inconsistent estimates of the structural slopes. Skrondal and Laake (2001) showed that the revised scheme, the regression score for an explanatory factor and the Bartlett score for a response factor, gives consistent estimates of every parameter of a latent regression model, provided the explanatory and the response factors are fitted as separate measurement models; scores from one joint model of both are not covered by that result and should not feed a regression among the same factors, and fitting each factor alone (factorwise) is consistent only in special cases such as the independent clusters model with one explanatory factor. Even then the standard errors the second step reports do not account for the scores having been estimated (corrected ones may require resampling), no conventional test of fit is available, and factor score regression works badly for nonlinear models such as polynomial regression. Devlieger, Mayer, and Rosseel (2016) compared regression and Bartlett factor score regression, the bias avoiding method of Skrondal and Laake, and the bias correcting method of Croon (2002). The bias avoiding method was unbiased for unstandardized but not for standardized coefficients and had the largest standard error bias of the four, and Croon's method, with the standard error they developed for it, was the only suitable alternative to structural equation modeling, comparable in bias, efficiency, mean squared error, power, and Type I error rate, though with more standard error bias. The differences among the methods disappeared when factor score indeterminacy was low, and they advise assessing it first, which the determinacy columns here allow. Croon's correction is local structural after measurement with the maximum likelihood mapping, whose matrix is the Bartlett score matrix (Rosseel & Loh, 2024), and Rosseel and Loh recommend local structural after measurement over one-step estimation when the sample is small to medium or the items have low to moderate reliability, with as many separate measurement blocks as the model permits. It is available as lavaan::sam(). Rosseel and Loh developed the framework for complete continuous data, so with missing data or ordered items its two-step standard errors deserve a check against a bootstrap.

Missing Data. Under full information maximum likelihood (missing = "ml"), lavaan scores each case from its own observed items, pattern by pattern, which is what \(o\) denotes above. For continuous items, the regression score so computed is the posterior weighted maximum likelihood estimate that Estabrook and Neale (2013) call full ML, and the Bartlett score so computed is their unweighted ML estimate. In their simulation (one factor), the two were equally reliable with complete data, and with missing values the posterior weighted score was the more reliable (with five items and values missing completely at random, a mean reliability of .780 against .767, and .752 for the scaled person mean), which they attribute to its empirical Bayes component. A case that answered none of a factor's items has no Bartlett score for that factor; its regression score is kept, but it comes only from the case's other observed variables, through the model (the items of correlated factors, a covariate that predicts the factor, an outcome the factor predicts), it is the factor's mean when none of them bears on the factor, and its determinacy says how little that is. A case with no observed variable has no score of either kind. Under listwise deletion the rows with a missing value were not used by the fit and are not scored; for continuous items, a fit with missing = "ml" scores them, unless the missing value is an exogenous covariate's. With fixed.x = TRUE, lavaan's default, every fit deletes a row whose covariate is missing, FIML with missing = "ml" included, except one with missing = "ml.x" (which a fit conditional on the covariates does not allow), and the reason column names that remedy; with ordered items no fit that lavaan can score keeps such a row. lavaan has no FIML for ordered items: fitted by WLSMV, they take their parameters from pairwise or listwise deletion, which assumes the values are missing completely at random, and under pairwise deletion (missing = "pairwise") the EBM and ML scores use each case's observed items, so that fit scores the rows listwise deletion leaves out.

A fit of continuous items that keeps the incomplete cases without FIML is scored the same way, each case from its own observed items, with the fit's estimates in the formulas above: a fit by two-stage maximum likelihood (lavaan's missing = "two.stage" or "robust.two.stage", as fa_confirmatory fits with missing = "two_stage") or by pairwise deletion (missing = "pairwise", or "available.cases", which for continuous items gives lavaan the same pairwise complete moments and estimates). The two-stage estimates are consistent when the values are missing at random, as the FIML estimates are (Savalei & Bentler, 2009); the estimates from pairwise deletion require the values to be missing completely at random. The scores treat the estimates as known, as they treat the FIML estimates, so the scores, standard errors, and determinacies of such a fit mean what they mean under FIML and differ from FIML's only as the estimates differ. A fit without a mean structure (the default for one group under pairwise deletion) centers its observed variables at their sample means and its factors at the means lavaan gives them (lavInspect(fit, "mean.lv")): zero, or for a factor a covariate predicts, the prediction at the covariate's mean, as a FIML fit has it. lavaan::lavPredict() scores such a fit as complete data, leaving every case with a missing value without a score, so these scores are computed here, by the closed forms lavPredict() applies pattern by pattern under FIML. Auxiliary variables of the first stage of a two-stage fit (lavaan's aux) are not in the model and do not enter the scores. Such a fit conditional on exogenous covariates (conditional.x = TRUE) is refused.

Missing values affect the two scores differently. Conditional unbiasedness of the Bartlett score and the coverage of its Wald interval are properties of its sampling distribution given the case's factor value, and with missing values they hold when, given the factors, whether an item is observed does not depend on the residuals of the items scored: values missing completely at random, or missing because of the factors themselves or of variables related to the items only through the factors. Rubin (1976) showed that sampling distribution inferences may ignore the process that causes missing data when the missing values are missing at random and the observed values are observed at random, whereas likelihood and Bayesian inferences need only the first (with the parameters of the process distinct from those of the data). Missingness that depends on the observed values of the factor's own items, the kind of missing at random that FIML is commonly used for, fails the second: it selects each pattern on those items' residuals, so the Bartlett score of a pattern is biased given the factor value, and its interval covers the factor value less often than stated in that pattern. In a one-factor model of four items with loadings of .7 and 5,000 cases, the last three items missing whenever the first fell below -0.3, the Bartlett scores of the cases left with one item averaged 0.82 below their factor values and their 95% intervals covered 92.7% of them; with as many values missing completely at random, -0.01 and 95.3%. The regression score is a posterior quantity, so missingness that depends only on what the score conditions on leaves its posterior interval with its average coverage (94.6% in the first case). Missingness that runs through an auxiliary variable the scores set aside (see Auxiliary Variables and Covariates) is not of that kind for the regression score, since the pattern then carries information about the factor beyond the observed items, and the regression score of a pattern is biased. The Bartlett score is not, but only when the auxiliary is related to the items through the factors alone (independent of them given the factors); one that shares variance with an item beyond the factor, as an earlier wave of the same item does, selects the pattern on that item's residual, which fails the condition above. In the same design with the last three items missing whenever an auxiliary fell below -0.3, an auxiliary that correlated .4 with the factor and with nothing else left the cases with one item Bartlett scores 0.05 below their factor values on average (within two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero), with intervals covering 95.6%, and regression scores 0.17 above them; one that correlated .4 with the factor and .5 with the first item's residual left them Bartlett scores 0.56 below their factor values, with intervals covering 93.1%. A score whose error has mean zero given the factor leaves the slopes of a regression in which it is the response unbiased, and that is the Bartlett score's place in the revised scheme of factor score regression above, so missingness that depends on the factor's own observed items weakens it there. The reliabilities of Estabrook and Neale (2013) quoted above are for values missing completely at random.

Determinacy. The determinacy of a score is its correlation with the factor, \([A \Lambda_o \Phi]_{kk} / \sqrt{[A \Sigma_{oo} A']_{kk} \Phi_{kk}}\) for the weight matrix \(A\) of the score, the formula lavaan uses for fs.determinacy and fs.determinacy.bartlett, evaluated here for each missing data pattern. Its square is the reliability of the score as a measure of the factor. The regression score has the larger determinacy, since it is the linear function of the observed items that correlates most with the factor; for a one-factor model the two are equal, and with uncorrelated residuals their square is coefficient H (Hancock & Mueller, 2001), the reliability of the optimally weighted composite of the items. Per-pattern determinacy shows the cost of each missing item. It is computed for continuous items; with ordered items each case's standard error is given instead. Beside the regression score's determinacy \(\rho\), the display and the determinacy and patterns attributes report \(2\rho^2 - 1\) (min_score_correlation), the lowest correlation that two sets of scores, each as consistent with the model as the other, can have (Guttman, 1955, as Grice, 2001, p. 435, presents it). It is zero when \(\rho^2 = .5\), where two such sets can be uncorrelated, and negative below that, so it says how far the scores of different cases can be trusted to order the cases on the factor. The package reports the quantity and draws no line.

Intervals. The interval around a regression score is a posterior (empirical Bayes) interval: its coverage holds on average over cases, not for each case's factor value. The interval around a Bartlett score is a Wald interval for the case's factor value. Both treat the model's estimated parameters as known, so they do not carry the parameters' sampling variability. For ordered items the EBM interval approximates the posterior around its mode, and the ML interval is a Wald interval. The ML score of a factor exists only when the likelihood of the case's responses has a finite maximum in it. A case whose observed items of a factor all sit at the same end of their scales (all in the lowest category, or all in the highest, for positive loadings) has none, since the likelihood keeps rising as the factor's value moves out. With items shared among factors (cross-loadings, a bifactor model) the likelihood can also rise without bound along a direction that moves several factors together, or stay flat along one that the observed items cannot separate. The check is exact: a factor has a finite and unique ML score when no direction along which no observed item's probability falls moves it, which a nonnegative least squares problem decides (by Farkas' lemma), and with simple structure it reduces to the rule for the items at an end. It reads each item's loadings as lavaan's likelihood does, including those of an observed variable regressed on the factors (an outcome the factor predicts, or an item with a direct effect of another factor), which lavaan holds among the regressions. A factor that fails it has its ML score and interval NA with the reason. A factor that passes it keeps its ML score, also when it shares observed items with a factor whose likelihood rises without bound: as that factor moves out, the shared items' probabilities tend to 1 whatever this factor's value, so its maximum is that of the case's other items, which lavaan's optimizer reaches within its tolerance (within 1.2e-4 of a direct maximization of the likelihood for the factor of a cross-loading item in the tests, and within 1.1% of the standard error in a bifactor model of 12 items). When lavaan's default optimizer stops on its iteration limit and returns no score for the case, the score comes from lavaan's nlminb optimizer. A higher order factor, which has no items of its own, has no ML score at all: the likelihood of the responses depends on the factors it measures, not on it, and lavaan's value is the center of the small ridge its optimizer adds. Its EBM score, which the factor's place in the model informs, is kept.

Ordered Items Need lavaan 0.7-3. The probability of an ordered response compares each threshold with the mean of the item's latent response, its intercept plus its loadings times the factor values. The EBM and ML scores of lavaan 0.7-2 counted the intercept twice in that comparison, so they were wrong in any model whose ordered indicators have intercepts other than zero (a multiple group model with equal thresholds, for one); lavaan 0.7-3 corrected it, and also changed how the scores treat the scale factors of the delta parameterization. A fit with ordered items is therefore refused under an older lavaan, with the remedy, rather than scored with numbers that may be wrong.

Multiple Groups. The scores use each group's own parameters, and the group column names the group. Scores from different groups are on a common metric only to the extent the measurement model is invariant across the groups (equal loadings for comparing relations that involve the scores, and equal intercepts as well for comparing their levels); see measurement_invariance. Rows whose group is missing are not used by the fit; with data they are kept, without a score.

Auxiliary Variables and Covariates. An observed variable that indicates no factor and enters the model only through covariances with the indicators is an auxiliary variable carried as a saturated correlate (Graham, 2003), as the reliability functions of this package carry them. It helps the estimates under missing data, but under that parameterization it is uncorrelated with every factor and correlated with the item residuals, so whatever it shares with the factor is carried as residual covariance, and a score that conditions on it subtracts true score variance. When such variables are present the scores are computed from the indicators alone, with the fit's estimates, the scored_from attribute is "indicators", and a message says so. A higher order factor, which has no items of its own, then has no Bartlett score, nor, when the data have missing values, in the scores computed here for a two-stage fit or one by pairwise deletion (missing = "pairwise" or "available.cases"), nor in a fit in which lavaan gives an observed variable a row of zeros among the loadings (see Observed Variables in Regressions): lavaan forms that score through the loadings of the factors it measures, a construction not repeated here, and the reason column says so; its regression score is computed as for any other factor. A covariate that predicts a factor (f ~ x) is different: the scores condition on it as the model specifies (as on any observed variable that enters a regression of the model), and Curran, Cole, Bauer, Hussong, and Gottfredson (2016) found that including such covariates in the scoring model improved score quality in nearly every condition of their simulation.

Observed Variables in Regressions. An observed variable regressed on others, such as an item with a direct effect of a covariate (y1 ~ x, the multiple indicators multiple causes model of differential item functioning) or an outcome the factor predicts (z ~ f), is held by lavaan as a latent variable measured by itself without error, with its loadings among the regressions and its residual variance among those of the latent variables. The scores, their standard errors and determinacies, the check of the ML score, and the check of the solution take its loadings and residual variance from there, as lavaan::lavPredict() does, so an item with a direct effect enters its factor's Bartlett score, which is then conditionally unbiased given the factor and the covariate. An observed variable that lavaan holds the same way but regresses on nothing, such as a criterion that covaries with a factor (f ~~ z) or a covariate of a factor that also covaries with another variable (so that lavaan does not count it among the exogenous covariates), is conditioned on, as an exogenous covariate is: the regression score is the factor's mean given it and the items, and the Bartlett score is conditionally unbiased given the factors and it. In a fit conditional on the covariates (conditional.x = TRUE) without regressions among the variables lavaan holds as latent (no \(B\) matrix), so is an observed variable regressed only on exogenous covariates (z ~ x): lavaan then keeps the variable's own row among the loadings, lavPredict()'s regression score is the factor's mean given the items, the variable, and the covariates, and its Bartlett score is conditionally unbiased given the factors, the variable, and the covariates, also when the variable covaries with a factor (f ~ x, z ~ x, f ~~ z; lavaan::sem() frees that covariance by default). In a model with regressions among them, lavPredict() gives a variable regressed on nothing a row of zeros among the loadings, which leaves its covariances with the factors out of the scores (with f ~ x and f ~~ z for three Holzinger and Swineford tests, its regression score missed the conditional mean by up to 1.9), so the scores of such a fit are computed here, with the formulas lavPredict() uses; one conditional on the covariates (conditional.x = TRUE) is refused, with the remedy. In a fit without a mean structure and without exogenous covariates, lavPredict() counts the mean of a variable held this way twice, as its intercept and as the mean of the latent variable that holds it, which shifts by a constant every score whose weights involve the variable: the regression score of every factor related to it and the Bartlett score of a factor that predicts it (for a factor of three Holzinger and Swineford spatial tests that predicts a fourth test and correlates .50 with a factor of three speed tests, by -0.39 and -0.61 for the first factor's regression and Bartlett scores and by -0.07 for the second factor's regression score); the scores of such a fit are computed here, with the formulas lavPredict() uses and the means the fit implies. A higher order factor's Bartlett score, which lavaan forms through the loadings of the factors it measures, is lavaan's less the constant the double count adds (-1.09 for a second order factor of three factors of three Holzinger and Swineford tests each, when the spatial factor predicts the paper form board test), so it equals that of the fit with a mean structure. In a model with regressions among the variables lavaan holds as latent, a variable regressed on others is represented by its measurement equation, with its disturbance as the error, which is right only when that disturbance is uncorrelated with the factors and with the variables the scores condition on, so a fit in which such a variable predicts a factor, directly or through others (an observed mediator), or has a residual covariance with a factor is refused: lavPredict() then gives a Bartlett score that is not conditionally unbiased and, when a factor is involved, a regression score that is not the factor's conditional mean (with f ~ a and a ~ x for three Holzinger and Swineford tests, it missed the conditional mean by up to 1.08, with a correlation of .92). Carried as a single indicator latent variable (A =~ a with a ~~ 0*a), such a variable is scored correctly: written so, lavaan fixes one scale constraint, the loading or, with std.lv = TRUE, the latent variable's variance, so the refitted model is the same model, with the refused fit's log likelihood and degrees of freedom (Bollen, 1989, Chapter 7). Written A =~ 1*a in a fit with std.lv = TRUE, it fixes both, which is a different model whose scores are not those of the refused one. In a multiple group fit, group.equal holds parameters equal by kind, and the variable's intercept, residual variance, and covariances become the latent variable's, so the refit is the same model only when it carries the refused fit's constraints across the groups: with equal intercepts, lavaan frees the latent variable's mean after the first group unless it is fixed at zero in every group (A ~ 0*1; for two schools with equal loadings and intercepts the refit without it had a log likelihood of -4246.42 on 15 degrees of freedom, against -4246.51 on 16), and the equalities group.equal places on residual variances and covariances, or on those of latent variables, must be given to the variable's parameters as the refused fit had them and to no others. The message says which apply.

With ordered items, lavaan's EBM and ML scores leave a direct effect of an exogenous covariate on an observed variable out of each case's likelihood, and they take an observed variable that is not an exogenous covariate as zero where it predicts another. That leaves the scores unchanged when the variable predicted depends on no factor directly: its density given its predictors then does not involve the factors, so the term left out changes each case's likelihood by a factor constant in them. Such fits are scored: a covariate's effect on an observed outcome unrelated to the factors (w ~ x), and a fully mediated chain of continuous observed variables (m ~ f with w ~ m, whose EBM and ML scores agree with a direct maximization of the model's likelihood for four Holzinger and Swineford tests cut at their quartiles). A fit in which the term left out involves the factors is refused: a direct effect on a variable that also depends on a factor directly (y1 ~ x for an item, whose thresholds are estimated given the covariate, so the scores are those of a case with the covariate at zero; ML scores off by 0.11 to 0.44 for an item regressed on age), a regression of such a variable on an observed one (y4 ~ y3 for local dependence between two items, ML scores off by up to 0.18 for the four tests; or w ~ m + f), a regression on an ordered item, whose latent response is not observed (w ~ y3), and a regression on an observed variable that a row the fit keeps lacks while it has the one predicted, where the missing variable depends on a factor through no variable the row has observed (pairwise deletion, where the model's likelihood of the variable predicted then runs through the missing one to the factors). A variable the row has observed on the way cuts that dependence, and the row is scored: with m ~ f, w ~ m, and s ~ w, a row lacking w but having m and s is scored, while a row lacking m but having w refuses the fit. A fit is refused, too, for an observed variable lavaan holds among the latent variables whose disturbance covaries with a factor, regressed on nothing or, in a fit without regressions among the latent variables, only on exogenous covariates (f ~ x with w ~ x, where lavaan::sem() frees the covariance of f and w by default): the EBM score takes the factor's prior from its model implied mean given the covariates, which leaves the variable's value out, so it is the posterior mode given the items and covariates alone; written as a predictor of the factor (f ~ x), a variable regressed on nothing is an exogenous covariate, which the EBM score conditions on. A fit with ordered items and exogenous covariates that is not conditional on them (conditional.x = FALSE), which lavPredict() cannot score, is refused as well. The EBM and ML scores of lavaan also take each case's likelihood as the product of its observed variables' probabilities given the factors, so they leave residual covariances among those variables out; a fit with one is scored with a warning, since its scores are those of the model without it (with a residual correlation of -0.12 between two of the four tests, the ML scores of the 160 response patterns differed from the scores that maximize the model's own likelihood by up to 0.11, 15% of their standard error, and by 0.03 at the median).

An improper solution is scored with a warning: one with a negative residual variance (a Heywood case, also of an observed variable regressed on others), a negative factor variance, a covariance matrix of the factors that is not positive definite (a factor correlation beyond 1, for one), a residual covariance matrix of the continuous variables scored from that is not positive definite, or, when none of these holds, a residual covariance matrix of the structural part of the model that is not, the conditions lavaan's post-estimation check flags. The regression weights use the model implied covariance matrix and the Bartlett weights the loadings and the inverse of the residual covariance matrix, so both scores inherit the solution. For ordered items lavaan computes no EBM or ML score for a solution with a negative residual variance, and the warning and the reason column say so.

Examples

data(holzinger_swineford)

# Two later spatial tests (t25, t26) were given to the Grant-White
# pupils only, so under full information maximum likelihood each
# Pasteur pupil (rows 1 to 156) is scored from four spatial tests and
# each Grant-White pupil from six.
model <- "
  spatial =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t3_paper_form_board +
             t4_lozenges + t25_paper_form_board_r + t26_flags
  verbal  =~ t5_general_information + t6_paragraph_comprehension +
             t7_sentence + t8_word_classification + t9_word_meaning"
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE,
                   missing = "ml")
fs <- factor_scores(fit, data = holzinger_swineford)
fs
#> Factor scores: regression and Bartlett scores, 2 factors (spatial, verbal), 301 rows
#> Fit: ML, missing = "ml"; scored from the fit
#> 
#>  row  factor regression    se           95% CI Bartlett   se           95% CI 
#>    1 spatial     -0.992 0.527  [-2.026, 0.041]   -1.488 0.652 [-2.766, -0.210]
#>    2 spatial     -0.302 0.527  [-1.336, 0.731]   -0.225 0.652  [-1.503, 1.053]
#>    3 spatial     -0.850 0.527  [-1.883, 0.184]   -0.797 0.652  [-2.075, 0.481]
#>    1  verbal     -0.166 0.284  [-0.723, 0.392]   -0.132 0.299  [-0.718, 0.453]
#>    2  verbal     -0.963 0.284 [-1.520, -0.406]   -1.057 0.299 [-1.642, -0.471]
#>    3  verbal     -2.051 0.284 [-2.608, -1.494]   -2.240 0.299 [-2.825, -1.654]
#> (the first 3 rows of each factor)
#> 
#> Determinacy, the correlation of each score with its factor, by missing data pattern; min_r, the lowest correlation two sets of scores equally consistent with the model can have (2 x the regression score's determinacy squared, minus 1; Guttman, 1955):
#>  pattern   n  factor items regression Bartlett min_r
#>        1 145 spatial   6/6      0.888    0.882 0.577
#>        1 145  verbal   5/5      0.959    0.958 0.839
#>        2 156 spatial   4/6      0.850    0.838 0.444
#>        2 156  verbal   5/5      0.959    0.958 0.838
#> 
#> Intervals treat the fitted parameters as known: regression intervals
#> are posterior (empirical Bayes) intervals, Bartlett intervals Wald
#> intervals for each case's factor value. In a later regression, use
#> regression scores for a predictor and Bartlett scores for an outcome,
#> each from its own measurement model (Skrondal & Laake, 2001); for
#> relations among factors, one-step SEM or structural after measurement
#> (lavaan::sam()) is preferred to any regression among scores.
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# One pupil from each school: the spatial scores of the Pasteur pupil
# rest on four tests and have the wider intervals.
fs[fs$row %in% c(1, 157),
   c("row", "factor", ".derived_regression",
     ".derived_regression_ci_lower", ".derived_regression_ci_upper",
     ".derived_bartlett", ".derived_bartlett_ci_lower",
     ".derived_bartlett_ci_upper", "items_observed", "items")]
#>  row factor  .derived_regression .derived_regression_ci_lower
#>  1   spatial -0.992              -2.026                      
#>  157 spatial -1.292              -2.193                      
#>  1   verbal  -0.166              -0.723                      
#>  157 verbal  -0.198              -0.755                      
#>  .derived_regression_ci_upper .derived_bartlett .derived_bartlett_ci_lower
#>  0.041                        -1.488            -2.766                    
#>  -0.391                       -1.729            -2.778                    
#>  0.392                        -0.132            -0.718                    
#>  0.358                        -0.153            -0.739                    
#>  .derived_bartlett_ci_upper items_observed items
#>  -0.210                     4              6    
#>  -0.680                     6              6    
#>  0.453                      5              5    
#>  0.433                      5              5    

# Determinacy and standard errors for each missing data pattern.
attr(fs, "patterns")
#>   group pattern  factor   n items_observed items
#> 1  <NA>       1 spatial 145              6     6
#> 2  <NA>       1  verbal 145              5     5
#> 3  <NA>       2 spatial 156              4     6
#> 4  <NA>       2  verbal 156              5     5
#>                   missing_variables determinacy_regression determinacy_bartlett
#> 1                                                0.8881010            0.8816139
#> 2                                                0.9588085            0.9581213
#> 3 t25_paper_form_board_r, t26_flags              0.8496532            0.8376594
#> 4 t25_paper_form_board_r, t26_flags              0.9587310            0.9581213
#>   min_score_correlation regression_se bartlett_se
#> 1             0.5774469     0.4596483   0.5353493
#> 2             0.8386274     0.2840533   0.2988793
#> 3             0.4438211     0.5273419   0.6520465
#> 4             0.8383304     0.2843146   0.2988793

# The table is ordered by factor and then row, so one factor's column
# lines up with the data.
spatial_bartlett <- fs$.derived_bartlett[fs$factor == "spatial"]
length(spatial_bartlett) == nrow(holzinger_swineford)
#> [1] TRUE

# When scores must stand in for factors in a regression, Skrondal and
# Laake (2001) pair the regression score of the predictor with the
# Bartlett score of the outcome, each from its own measurement model.
# With both factor variances fixed at 1 the slope estimates the latent
# correlation; pairing the regression scores attenuates it. The lm()
# standard errors treat the scores as error free and are not valid.
fit_v <- lavaan::cfa("verbal =~ t5_general_information +
  t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t8_word_classification +
  t9_word_meaning", data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE,
  missing = "ml")
fit_s <- lavaan::cfa("spatial =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes +
  t3_paper_form_board + t4_lozenges + t25_paper_form_board_r +
  t26_flags", data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE,
  missing = "ml")
fs_v <- factor_scores(fit_v)
fs_s <- factor_scores(fit_s)
c(revised = unname(coef(lm(fs_s$.derived_bartlett ~
                              fs_v$.derived_regression))[2]),
  regression_both = unname(coef(lm(fs_s$.derived_regression ~
                                      fs_v$.derived_regression))[2]),
  latent = lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv")["spatial", "verbal"])
#>         revised regression_both          latent 
#>       0.4336799       0.3212779       0.4621871 

# The broom verbs: the table as a plain data frame, and one summary row.
head(generics::tidy(fs))
